name: Slav: Czech Variation
summary: The Czech (main-line) Slav, 4...dxc4 5.a4 Bf5, develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6, and White fights to regain the pawn and play e4.
intro: The Czech Variation is the classical main line of the Slav Defence, reached after 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 dxc4 5.a4 Bf5. With 4...dxc4 Black captures the gambit pawn, and after 5.a4 — restraining the ...b5 that would try to cling to the extra material — Black develops the light-squared bishop actively to f5, outside the pawn chain, before playing ...e6. This is the whole point of the Slav over the Queen's Gambit Declined: the c8-bishop, so often a problem piece, reaches a good diagonal before being shut in. White, meanwhile, will regain the pawn on c4 in due course and use the space gained by a4 to fight for the central e4 break. The result is one of the most respected and thoroughly mapped openings in chess, a regular guest at the very highest level.
line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The defining feature of the Slav is that Black supports the d5-pawn with ...c6 rather than ...e6, keeping the diagonal of the light-squared bishop open. After 4...dxc4 5.a4 Bf5 that bishop takes up an excellent post on f5, eyeing the b1-h7 diagonal, and only then does Black play ...e6 to complete a solid, harmonious structure. The a4-pawn is a double-edged concession: it stops ...b5 and gains queenside space, but it also weakens the b4-square, which Black can exploit with ...Bb4 and ...Nbd7. The middlegame is a classic struggle between White's central and spatial ambitions and Black's rock-solid, well-coordinated setup.

Both sides manoeuvre around the key central breaks. White wants to prepare and play e4, when a broad pawn centre and active pieces promise an edge; Black restrains it, completes development with ...e6, ...Bb4 or ...Be7, and ...O-O, and looks to strike back with ...c5 or ...e5 at the right moment. The bishop on f5 is both an asset and, occasionally, a target, since White can gain time with Nh4 to challenge it or expand with a well-timed advance. Endgames are never far away, and the resulting positions demand accurate handling from both players.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The most important continuation is 6.e3, preparing Bxc4 and a build-up toward e4. After 6...e6 7.Bxc4 Bb4, the pin on the c3-knight and the well-placed f5-bishop give Black a comfortable game; play often continues 8.O-O O-O 9.Qe2, when White dreams of e4 and Black reacts precisely, frequently with ...Bg6 and ...Nbd7. This whole complex, known as the Dutch Variation, has been analysed exhaustively and is the theoretical backbone of the modern Slav.

The other principal try is the sharp 6.Ne5, the Krause Variation, posting the knight aggressively and challenging Black to react. After 6...Nbd7 7.Nxc4 the play takes on a more concrete character, with mutual chances in the centre. White can also insert 6.Nh4, aiming to win the bishop pair by capturing on f5 and accepting some structural loosening in return. Each of these approaches gives the Czech Slav a distinct flavour, but in all of them Black's fundamental soundness has kept the defence at the forefront of opening theory.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Slav Defence rose to prominence in the 1920s and 1930s and became a central battleground of world-championship chess in the matches between Alexander Alekhine and Max Euwe, the latter a great connoisseur of the ...dxc4 and ...Bf5 lines. Its solidity and the healthy development of the light-squared bishop made it a natural choice for players seeking a fully sound answer to the Queen's Gambit.

In the decades since, the Czech main line has been employed and enriched by a long list of World Champions, including Mikhail Botvinnik, Vasily Smyslov, and later Viswanathan Anand and Vladimir Kramnik, whose 2008 title match featured deep Slav theory. It remains a staple of elite repertoires and of correspondence and engine analysis alike, a byword for reliability that still offers both sides room to play for a win.
